passage.title: Text One: Market Morning
paras: At five in the morning the market is still deciding what it will be. Crates thump onto trestles. Someone is singing, badly, behind the fish stall. By six, the oranges are stacked in careful pyramids and the first customers arrive, mostly older people who know that the best of everything goes early. Nobody hurries them. Mr Osei, who has sold vegetables here for thirty-one years, saves the softest tomatoes for a widow who cannot chew well. "A market," he tells me, "is a village that meets every day."

passage.title: Text Two: A Morning at the Market
paras: The market was a scene of such noise and plenty as I had never witnessed. Carts pressed upon carts; porters bore baskets piled so high upon their heads that they seemed to walk beneath small mountains of cabbages. The poor came at the closing hour, when the sellers, weary and wishing to be home, let go their bruised fruit for a halfpenny. I observed a flower-girl, not above ten years old, give away her last violets to a crying child, and I thought her the richest person in the place.

head: Question
Answer
rows: Any two: carried baskets on their heads; sold bruised fruit cheaply; wanted to go home

passage.title: Model
paras: The writer presents the market as a living community. Personification ('the market is still deciding what it will be') makes it seem to wake like a person, while the sounds of crates that 'thump' and someone 'singing, badly' add affectionate humour. The quiet detail of Mr Osei saving 'the softest tomatoes for a widow who cannot chew well' shifts the focus from trade to care, and his final words, 'a village that meets every day', sum up the writer's view.

passage.title: Model
paras: The nineteenth-century writer piles up noise and plenty: carts 'pressed upon carts' and porters walk 'beneath small mountains of cabbages', a hyperbolic image of abundance. The structure moves from the crowd to the poor at 'the closing hour', and finally to the flower-girl who gives away her last violets. The paradox that he thought her 'the richest person in the place' turns material wealth upside down.

passage.title: Model
paras: Both writers find the true value of a market in small acts of kindness rather than goods, but whereas the modern writer hears it in Mr Osei's own words, the nineteenth-century observer sees it in a silent gift. The modern text is warm and gently comic; the older text is grander and more formal, its long sentences reflecting the crowds of its time.
